question: In June 1776, the Continental Congress named a 'Committee of Five' to write a declaration of independence. But they did not write it as a group. They gave the job to their youngest member, a man of just 33. Which member wrote the Declaration of Independence?
context: The Committee of Five (appointed June 11, 1776) was Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman, and Robert R. Livingston, but the writing fell to the 33-year-old Jefferson. Source: National Archives, The Declaration of Independence: A History, archives.gov/founding-docs/declaration-history.

question: Around the year 820, a scholar in Baghdad named al-Khwarizmi wrote a mathematics book whose Arabic title used the word 'al-jabr.' That word describes the move of shifting a subtracted term across an equation. A whole branch of mathematics still carries that Arabic word as its name. Which branch?
context: ALGEBRA comes straight from al-Khwarizmi's word 'al-jabr' (restoration — moving terms across an equation), paired with 'al-muqabala' (balancing — cancelling like terms). His book was the first to teach solving equations as its own subject. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi.

question: For over a thousand years the great walled city of Constantinople had been the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, guarding the crossing between Europe and Asia. In 1453 a 21-year-old Ottoman Turkish sultan named Mehmed II laid a fierce siege to it — and captured it. The deed gave him a single nickname that the Ottoman world used for him ever after. What was it?
context: Mehmed II (born 30 March 1432) was forever after called 'Fatih' — 'the Conqueror' — for taking the city on 29 May 1453, ending a Roman state that traced its line back to Constantine the Great founding the city in 330 AD. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmed_II
